title: Teotihuacan
capsule: Teotihuacan was the largest pre-Columbian city in the Americas before the Aztec period, located in the Basin of Mexico roughly 40 km northeast of modern Mexico City; by its Xolalpan peak around 400–550 CE it held 100,000–200,000 inhabitants within a planned urban grid of approximately 18 km², anchored by the Avenue of the Dead and the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its rulers — whose names remain unknown, as no indigenous script has been deciphered — dominated highland Mesoamerican obsidian trade and projected political influence into the Maya lowlands, as demonstrated by the 378 CE arrival of Teotihuacan military agents at Tikal that displaced the ruling dynasty. Around 550 CE elite precincts along the Avenue of the Dead were systematically burned in what the archaeological record suggests was an internal uprising rather than foreign conquest, after which the city rapidly depopulated and successor powers including Xochicalco and Tula emerged.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The urban core is archaeologically well mapped; the political territory and extent of tributary control are inferred from artifact distributions and epigraphy and remain subjects of active scholarly debate, making precise territorial bounds speculative.
